action_items: Markus Klein — Email NorthStarApps: retry/disconnect guidance snippet + recommended backoff parameters — Due 2025-02-21
Renee Sullivan — Share TypeScript validation example (Zod) and Python (Pydantic) mapping for the same JSON schema — Due 2025-02-21

summary: Redwood walked NorthStarApps through the refreshed agentic workflow quickstart template demonstrating: (1) streaming response assembly, (2) tool calling with partial argument deltas and tool-result messages, and (3) structured output using a JSON schema plus runtime validation. NorthStarApps asked detailed questions about retry behavior on stream disconnects, how to validate structured output safely (especially when models occasionally emit invalid JSON), and compatibility differences vs OpenAI-style tool calling. Redwood emphasized: validate tool args before execution, treat streaming as an event log (don’t parse partial JSON mid-stream unless you know what you’re doing), and implement bounded retries with idempotent tool execution and clear fallback behavior.
topics: Quickstart overview: agent loop, tool registry, and structured output response format
Streaming event handling: deltas vs final, assembling message text, logging and error branches
Tool calling: partial tool-call args during streaming, parallel tool calls, tool-result message shape
Structured output: JSON schema constraints, validation, and retry/fallback strategy on invalid JSON
Compatibility: differences when using Redwood API vs OpenAI-compat endpoints
Deployment notes: Hosted vs Dedicated, VPC/private considerations, observability hooks
questions: What do we do if the stream drops mid tool-call and we only have partial arguments?
Do you recommend retrying the whole generation, or resuming the stream?
How strict is schema-constrained output across models? What’s actually guaranteed?
If we validate JSON and it fails, what’s the best prompt/retry pattern without doubling latency?
Are tool-call payloads identical to OpenAI’s? If not, what should we code against?
transcript:
Meeting: NorthStarApps — agentic quickstart walkthrough (streaming + tools + structured output)
Recorded: 2025-02-20 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees:
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Renee Sullivan (Redwood Inference, Developer Advocate)
- Jean-Paul Laurent (Redwood Inference, Quickstarts/Onboarding)
- Jamie Park (NorthStarApps, Staff Software Engineer)
- Lina Gomez (NorthStarApps, PM)
- Arun Iyer (NorthStarApps, ML Engineer)

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, I think it’s recording. Hey everyone. Thanks for making the time. Today we said we’d do a hands-on walkthrough of the updated agentic quickstart, specifically streaming plus tools plus structured output.

[00:12] Lina Gomez: Yep, thanks. We’ve been trying to stitch this together from like three different code samples, so I’m happy you all have a canonical one now.

[00:20] Renee Sullivan: Yeah, totally. That’s exactly why we did the refresh. The template is basically “copy/paste, it runs” and it demonstrates the patterns we want folks to use.

[00:30] Jamie Park: Great. Our main pain last time was, uh, tool call arguments getting cut off and then our tool executor would crash.

[00:38] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s a common one. We’ll show how we handle partial tool args and validation before calling the tool.

[00:46] Arun Iyer: And I want to see the structured output part. We tried JSON mode elsewhere and it still produced invalid JSON sometimes.

[00:54] Renee Sullivan: Yep. Same reality here: schema constraints help, but you still have to validate and have a retry/fallback strategy.

[01:02] Markus Klein: Alright, I’m gonna share my screen.

[01:06] (screen share) Markus Klein: You should see the repo. This is the agentic-workflow template. There are three key files: the agent loop, the tool registry, and the schema/validation helpers.

[01:21] Jean-Paul Laurent: And just a note, we updated the README to list env vars explicitly. So it’s like REDWOOD_API_KEY, optional base URL if you’re using a private gateway, and the model name.

[01:34] Jamie Park: We’re using TypeScript. That’s what you’re showing, right?

[01:37] Renee Sullivan: Yep, TypeScript today. The Python and Go ones are basically the same mental model though.

[01:45] Markus Klein: So first: streaming. We treat the stream as an event log. You’ll see event types come in: message deltas, tool-call deltas, and then a final message event.

[02:00] Jamie Park: Are those literally named that in the SDK or that’s conceptual?

[02:05] Markus Klein: Conceptual, but they map closely to what you’ll see in the SDK event union. The important thing is: don’t assume you get one big blob. You assemble it.

[02:16] Renee Sullivan: And specifically for tool calling: arguments can arrive as a sequence of partial strings. So you buffer them, then at “tool_call_complete” you parse JSON.

[02:26] Arun Iyer: That’s exactly what broke us. We were parsing on every chunk.

[02:30] Markus Klein: Yeah. So in this quickstart we basically do:
- if event is tool_call_delta: append to buffer keyed by tool_call_id
- if event is tool_call_end: parse once, validate args, then execute

[02:46] Lina Gomez: What about parallel tool calls? Our use case might call two services.

[02:51] Renee Sullivan: We include a pattern for parallel calls. The model can request multiple tool calls. In the template we show running them with Promise.all, but still collecting results and then sending tool-result messages back.

[03:06] Markus Klein: Right. And you’ll notice we keep each tool result associated with the tool_call_id so the model can correlate.

[03:14] Jamie Park: Is that required? Like, can we just push messages?

[03:18] Markus Klein: It’s strongly recommended. Otherwise you can get weird behavior if tools return out of order.

[03:25] Jean-Paul Laurent: Also the example includes a guard: if the tool result is too large we summarize it. Just to avoid dumping huge payloads back in.

[03:34] Arun Iyer: Okay. Can you run it?

[03:36] Markus Klein: Yep. So the demo prompt is “Find the top 3 customer support issues for streaming tool calls and propose fixes” — and the tool is a fake “searchTickets” that returns canned data.

[03:50] (terminal) Markus Klein: Running “pnpm dev”.

[03:55] (audio) Renee Sullivan: While it starts, I’ll call out the structured output piece. There’s a schema called “ReportSchema” and we ask the model to return an object with fields like summary, issues array, and remediation steps. Then we validate with Zod.

[04:12] Jamie Park: Is Zod required?

[04:14] Renee Sullivan: No, just an example. You can use ajv, zod, valibot, whatever. Key is: validate before you trust it.

[04:22] Markus Klein: Okay it’s up. I’m gonna kick it off.

[04:27] (console output) Markus Klein: You’ll see streaming tokens, then a tool call.

[04:31] Markus Klein: Here: “assistant.delta” events. We’re appending text.

[04:38] (console output) Markus Klein: Now we see tool call start… it’s requesting “searchTickets” with arguments. You can see they’re coming in pieces.

[04:48] Jamie Park: Yeah, that’s the part. So you’re literally seeing like '{"query": "tool call arg trunc…'

[04:56] Markus Klein: Exactly. We do NOT parse here.

[05:00] Arun Iyer: Do you ever get invalid JSON chunks? Like broken quotes mid-stream?

[05:05] Markus Klein: Yep, mid-stream it’s often not valid. That’s why we buffer as a raw string until the end.

[05:12] Renee Sullivan: And we also log if we see “partial_args” past a certain size. It’s a signal the model might be struggling.

[05:20] Lina Gomez: So then it calls the tool.

[05:22] Markus Klein: Yep. Tool executed, now we send back a tool-result message: role=tool, tool_call_id=..., content=...

[05:33] Markus Klein: Then the model continues the assistant message and finishes with a structured output object.

[05:39] (console output) Markus Klein: Here’s the final. It prints a JSON object.

[05:44] Arun Iyer: And you validate it?

[05:46] Renee Sullivan: Yep. See: “schema validation passed.” If it fails, we do a bounded retry.

[05:55] Jamie Park: What does bounded mean in your example?

[05:58] Renee Sullivan: Two attempts total. Attempt 1: normal. If JSON parse or schema validation fails, we re-ask with a short corrective instruction and the original schema. Attempt 2: if it still fails, we fallback to non-structured response and we return an error to the app layer.

[06:15] Arun Iyer: So you’re not infinite looping.

[06:17] Renee Sullivan: Yeah, please don’t infinite loop. Cost and latency blow up. Also you want predictable behavior.

[06:25] Lina Gomez: How do you prevent hallucinated tools? Like model calls a tool that doesn’t exist.

[06:31] Markus Klein: We validate tool name against a registry. If it’s unknown, we return a tool error result message like “tool not found”, and we instruct the agent loop to stop or ask the model to pick a valid tool.

[06:45] Jamie Park: Okay, now the big one: retries on stream disconnects. We saw a disconnect mid tool call. What should we do? Retry the request? Resume?

[06:56] Markus Klein: Great question. So, today, you should treat a stream disconnect as: you may have an incomplete assistant turn. There isn’t a guaranteed resume token. The safest strategy is to retry the whole generation with the conversation state you have.

[07:12] Jamie Park: But what if we already executed the tool? That’s the scary part.

[07:15] Markus Klein: Exactly. So you need idempotency on tools. Two approaches:
1) Make your tools idempotent with a request id. If you retry, the tool can say “already processed”.
2) Or, don’t execute tool calls until you have a complete tool call event. If the stream drops before tool_call_end, you should not execute.

[07:36] Arun Iyer: What if it drops after tool_call_end but before we receive the final assistant text?

[07:41] Markus Klein: Then you might have executed tool once. If you retry, the model might request it again. That’s where idempotency keys help. In the template we show generating a deterministic “tool_execution_id” from conversation_id + tool_call_id.

[07:58] Renee Sullivan: And we include a note: store “executed tool calls” in memory (or DB) for the session to avoid double execution.

[08:08] Jamie Park: Yeah, we can do that. So in your quickstart, are you doing actual retries in streaming?

[08:15] Jean-Paul Laurent: We show the pattern but keep it simple. Basically “try stream -> if network error, retry once with backoff”. We don’t try to merge partial deltas.

[08:27] Lina Gomez: That makes sense.

[08:30] Arun Iyer: How about structured output during streaming? Like, can we parse JSON incrementally to start rendering?

[08:37] Renee Sullivan: You can, but it’s footgun city. The recommended approach in docs is: don’t incrementally parse unless you have a real reason. Wait for final message, then parse.

[08:48] Markus Klein: And some models will emit trailing commentary unless you strongly instruct. So we do “Return ONLY valid JSON that matches this schema. No extra keys.” But again, validate.

[09:02] Arun Iyer: When validation fails, what’s the prompt you use? Like do you include the error message?

[09:08] Renee Sullivan: Yep, lightly. We include: “Your last output failed validation: <short error>. Output MUST be valid JSON matching schema.” Avoid pasting enormous stack traces.

[09:20] Jamie Park: Okay. Compatibility question: we currently have some code built around OpenAI tool calling. How different is Redwood’s shape?

[09:30] Markus Klein: The Redwood API supports tool calling, and we also have an OpenAI-compat endpoint. But there are differences. In particular, don’t assume exact same event names or chunk shapes when streaming.

[09:44] Jamie Park: So if we use your native SDK, we should code to your event union types.

[09:48] Markus Klein: Exactly. Use the native SDK and the canonical pattern. If you use OpenAI-compat, we can share the compatibility notes. Some folks mix and match and then examples don’t line up.

[10:02] Lina Gomez: Our org likes OpenAI-compat because we can swap providers.

[10:07] Markus Klein: Totally fair. Just be explicit in the code path: “compat mode” vs “native mode”. The quickstart is native mode because it gives best ergonomics and fewer surprises.

[10:20] Arun Iyer: Is structured output equally supported across models? Like if we pick a cheaper model, will it obey schema?

[10:28] Renee Sullivan: Not equally. Generally, bigger instruction-following models do better. The docs include a support matrix by model family. In practice, schema adherence is a spectrum.

[10:42] Arun Iyer: So you won’t guarantee 100%.

[10:44] Renee Sullivan: Correct. We can’t guarantee the model never outputs invalid JSON. We can guarantee the platform will pass through what the model emits and give you the tools to validate and retry.

[10:56] Jamie Park: That’s honest, thanks.

[11:00] Markus Klein: One more quick thing: tool argument validation. We show validating tool args against a schema too. So you don’t get “callPayments({amount: ‘ten’})” or whatever.

[11:14] Jamie Park: Are you using JSON schema for tool args too?

[11:18] Renee Sullivan: In TS we use Zod for tool args and also for structured output. But again, you can use JSON schema. The key is: validate tool args before executing, and if invalid, return tool error result.

[11:32] Lina Gomez: So the loop is: model -> tool call -> validate -> tool -> tool result -> model -> final structured output.

[11:39] Markus Klein: Yep.

[11:41] Arun Iyer: What about multiple tool calls in one assistant turn? Like it calls tool A and tool B.

[11:48] Markus Klein: Supported. The stream can contain multiple tool calls. The template supports collecting them and executing in parallel, then feeding results back.

[12:01] Jamie Park: Does the model ever interleave tool call args with assistant text?

[12:05] Markus Klein: It can. Usually you’ll see it switch into tool mode, but yes, there can be some mixed deltas. That’s why we keep separate buffers per message and per tool call.

[12:19] Renee Sullivan: And the template logs every event type so debugging is easier. Support tickets often come in without logs, and it’s hard.

[12:28] Lina Gomez: Speaking of support, what’s the typical guidance if we get invalid JSON output? Just retry?

[12:35] Renee Sullivan: Retry with correction once or twice. If it’s frequent, pick a different model or adjust prompt. Also reduce temperature.

[12:45] Arun Iyer: Do you recommend temperature 0 for schema output?

[12:48] Markus Klein: Usually yes, or close to it. For tool calling and schema output, determinism is your friend.

[12:56] Jamie Park: Okay. Cost question—if we do retries, cost doubles.

[13:02] Markus Klein: It can. That’s why bounded retries. Also you can do a cheap “repair pass” by asking a smaller model to fix malformed JSON, but you need to be careful.

[13:14] Arun Iyer: Interesting. Like “take this string and output valid JSON” kind of thing.

[13:18] Renee Sullivan: Exactly. We mention that as an option, but we don’t bake it into the quickstart because it complicates things.

[13:27] Lina Gomez: Another compatibility thing: we use AWS Bedrock for some stuff. Can we keep the same agent loop?

[13:34] Markus Klein: Conceptually yes. But our loop depends on the semantics of streaming tool call deltas. Some providers only give final tool call args. Our recommendation: use our canonical event model and adapt other providers to it, if you want portability.

[13:53] Jamie Park: That’s probably what we’ll do.

[13:56] Markus Klein: Cool. Let’s jump to the retry example code for disconnects.

[14:02] (screen share) Markus Klein: This function “runWithRetry”. It wraps stream consumption. On network errors it waits 250ms, then 1s, then stops. It also increments a “stream_disconnect” counter.

[14:18] Arun Iyer: Counter where? Like logs?

[14:20] Markus Klein: Just console + you can wire to your metrics. We added it because it’s useful in CI smoke tests too.

[14:28] Jamie Park: So if stream disconnects mid tool call, you discard partial args.

[14:33] Markus Klein: Yes. You do NOT execute tool. On retry, the model will regenerate tool call.

[14:40] Lina Gomez: What about user experience? They see partial output and then it restarts.

[14:46] Renee Sullivan: You can buffer and only display once you have a stable chunk, or show “reconnecting…” depending on your UX. But from a correctness standpoint, re-running is safer.

[15:00] Jamie Park: Okay. Now, can we see where you do schema validation for the final output?

[15:06] Renee Sullivan: Sure. Here. We take the final assistant message content. We do JSON.parse. If it throws, we treat it as validation error. Then Zod parse.

[15:18] Arun Iyer: Do you strip code fences? Sometimes models wrap JSON in ```.

[15:23] Renee Sullivan: Yep. We have a helper: remove leading/trailing fences and whitespace. But we try to prompt it not to do that.

[15:33] Jamie Park: That’s helpful.

[15:36] Markus Klein: Also note: we keep the raw text for debugging. If validation fails, we log the raw output and the error.

[15:45] Lina Gomez: For privacy, we’d need to be careful logging full content.

[15:48] Markus Klein: Right. For production, redact. In the example it’s just local.

[15:55] Arun Iyer: How do you handle tool result messages? Are they part of the same “messages” array?

[16:01] Markus Klein: Yes. Conversation is a list of messages. When tool call happens, you append a tool message. Then the next model call includes that.

[16:12] Jamie Park: So the agent loop is like: call model -> if tool_calls -> execute -> append tool messages -> call model again until no more.

[16:21] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[16:23] Lina Gomez: And streaming is only for the model call, not for the tool calls.

[16:28] Markus Klein: Right.

[16:30] Arun Iyer: Do you support streaming tool results back to the model? Probably not.

[16:34] Markus Klein: Not as a first-class feature, no. You can chunk tool results yourself if needed, but it’s rare.

[16:44] Jamie Park: You mentioned OpenAI-compat differences. Like what specifically?

[16:49] Markus Klein: Mostly: payload shapes and event naming. Some fields might be in different places. And parallel tool calls semantics. We’ll send a doc link after.

[17:02] Renee Sullivan: Also, don’t assume “function_call” vs “tool_call” naming. Our docs standardize on “tool” because it’s not just functions.

[17:12] Lina Gomez: Okay. That seems manageable.

[17:16] Markus Klein: Anything else you want to see? We can walk through adding a second tool quickly.

[17:22] Jamie Park: Maybe not now. But can you show how you define a tool schema?

[17:27] Renee Sullivan: Yep. Here’s the tool definition: name, description, and args schema. The model sees a JSON schema-ish description. Then at runtime we validate with Zod.

[17:40] Arun Iyer: So it’s like dual: descriptive schema for the model, and strict schema for runtime.

[17:46] Renee Sullivan: Exactly.

[17:48] Lina Gomez: And what about tool result schema? Do you enforce that?

[17:53] Markus Klein: We don’t enforce platform-side. But in your app, you can validate your own tool outputs before returning to the model. If your tool is buggy, you don’t want to confuse the model.

[18:06] Jamie Park: Got it.

[18:09] Arun Iyer: One more thing: can you run this in a VPC deployment? We’re not there yet, but eventually.

[18:17] Markus Klein: Yes. The same SDK works; you just point base URL to your private endpoint and configure networking. The template supports base URL override.

[18:28] Lina Gomez: Good.

[18:30] Markus Klein: Okay, let’s do recap and next steps.

[18:35] Markus Klein: We showed the agentic quickstart with: streaming event assembly, tool calling with partial args buffering, and structured output with schema validation + bounded retries. Your main next step is to run it in your environment and try your real tools.

[18:51] Renee Sullivan: I’ll send you the TS validation snippets and also the Python mapping since you said you might have a Python service.

[18:59] Jean-Paul Laurent: And I’ll double-check the README env var list and send the exact command we ran today.

[19:05] Jamie Park: Perfect.

[19:07] Lina Gomez: Can we also get guidance on the retry backoff numbers? We don’t want to hammer.

[19:12] Markus Klein: Yep, I’ll email a recommendation. Usually exponential backoff with jitter, one retry for interactive use, maybe two for background.

[19:21] Arun Iyer: And the model recommendations for structured output.

[19:25] Renee Sullivan: Yep, we’ll include that. Bigger models behave better. We’ll point to the support matrix.

[19:32] Markus Klein: Awesome. Thanks all. We’ll follow up with links and schedule the follow-up.

[19:38] (call ends)

Note: Fireflies transcript timestamps are approximate; speaker attribution may be imperfect in a few spots due to crosstalk and screen-share audio.
